messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  (none)

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miguel Alvarez is a 58-year-old forensic analyst who came to treatment nearly a year after an industrial explosion at a municipal evidence storage facility where he had been sent to assist with post-blast identification and scene reconstruction. He still describes the day in sharply sensory fragments: the metallic smell in the air, the pulverized concrete coating his shoes, the sudden secondary bang that sent everyone around him ducking, and the unnerving uncertainty about whether the structure was stable or whether something else had been planted. Because the disaster was caused by human action rather than accident, what stayed with him most was the conviction that danger could be hidden inside ordinary places, waiting behind a locked door or inside a building that looked routine from the outside. He had spent his career entering scenes methodically, trusting procedure and training, and the experience unsettled that trust at its core.

In the weeks afterward, Miguel noticed that his body no longer seemed to stand down. He sat at his desk in the forensic lab with his shoulders tight and jaw clenched, as if bracing for another blast without realizing it until hours had passed. Sudden sounds in the office—a dropped metal tray, a slammed file drawer, the sharp buzz of a security gate—made him jolt hard enough that coworkers began to glance over. He found himself scanning hallways, exits, and unfamiliar faces before he could focus on casework. Even at home, his wife noticed that he seemed wound up, turning quickly toward noises from the street and reacting as though he had been interrupted in the middle of something dangerous.

Miguel had also come to see the world in harsher terms. He was certain now that the world was dangerous, not in an abstract way but in the specific sense that ordinary settings could not be trusted. A warehouse, a parking garage, a courthouse annex—any place he did not know well felt impossible to relax in because he could not assess what might happen there. He began declining invitations that required going somewhere new, telling friends and family that he was tired or busy. When his department rotated assignments to unfamiliar buildings, he tried to trade tasks or asked for floor plans in advance, lingering over entry points and exits in a way that he once would have considered excessive. If he could not picture the space beforehand, he preferred not to go at all. At work this became increasingly noticeable, because forensic analysis occasionally required him to consult on scenes outside his usual lab environment. The prospect of stepping into a new site made his chest tighten before he had even left the office.

What troubled him almost as much as the fear itself was what he believed it said about him. Miguel had always thought of himself as steady, the person younger staff sought out when a case was gruesome or complicated. Now he had come to believe that his reactions proved he was a lousy coper. He judged himself for the way he startled, for how carefully he mapped exits, for the excuses he made to avoid unfamiliar locations. He said with visible shame that other men had been at that disaster too and had “moved on,” while he was still acting like his body had not gotten the message. Beneath that was a deeper loss: he feared he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. He had built an identity around precision, calm, and competence under pressure, and it felt humiliating to wonder whether that version of himself was gone.

Over the following months, these beliefs narrowed his life. Miguel kept to predictable routes, familiar restaurants, and the same grocery store aisle pattern, not because these routines gave him pleasure but because they reduced the strain of having to judge an unknown environment. His wife wanted to take weekend trips, but he resisted anywhere he had not been before. In the lab, he remained highly knowledgeable and meticulous, yet he increasingly tried to stay with bench analysis rather than field-related duties. He noticed this retreat and interpreted it as further evidence that he was diminished, which left him more discouraged and more preoccupied with how unsafe everything felt. Even small disruptions—construction noise outside the building, an alarm test, a stranger entering a secure area unexpectedly—could leave him keyed up for hours.

By the time Miguel sought help, the strain had become difficult to hide. A recent assignment to review evidence in an unfamiliar county facility left him so tense beforehand that he barely slept, and when a metal cart crashed in the corridor he recoiled so sharply that a junior colleague asked if he was all right. That moment embarrassed him more than he expected. He came in saying he was tired of feeling on edge and tired of arranging his life around places he could not fully control. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was simply who he was now: a man no longer able to trust the world, or himself. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to walk into a new place without feeling his whole body prepare for disaster.
